notes: Ruling slot 23 = Solomonic dynasty (Haile Selassie). No Derg (founded 1974). Imperial Bodyguard in 0 (Western-trained praetorian guard), ELF in 7 (armed, Arab-backed, anti-Western). MEISON (formed abroad 1968) in 4; EPRP not used (1972). Council of Ministers under Aklilu Habte-Wold in 13. MD sprites reused only for dynasty (23) and army (22).

0.name: Kebur Zebegna
0.text:
The Imperial Bodyguard is the elite division guarding the Emperor and the capital, trained by Swedish officers and equipped with American arms. In December 1960 its commander Mengistu Neway led a failed coup; the guard was purged and rebuilt under officers of proven loyalty.

The guard stands for the throne, order in Addis Ababa and close alliance with the United States, which keeps the Kagnew communications station in Asmara. Yet its officers remember 1960 and include men who want a modernized, efficient state. Its leverage lies in its control of the palace and the capital.

1.name: Yehizb Tewekayoch Mekir Bet
1.text:
The Chamber of Deputies is the elected lower house of the imperial parliament under the 1955 constitution. Political parties are not permitted, and the deputies returned in the 1969 elections are mostly landowners, local notables and wealthy merchants elected on personal standing.

The chamber defends property, the existing land tenure and the gradual development of the empire in partnership with the West. It has blocked land-reform bills that would protect tenants, while occasionally challenging ministers over budgets and corruption. Its leverage lies in its legal role over taxation and in the provincial gentry it represents.

2.name: Ye-Lewt Feligoch
2.text:
Ye-Lewt Feligoch are the Western-educated aristocrats and technocrats who want the monarchy reformed from within. Their most prominent figure is Lij Endalkachew Makonnen, a minister of noble birth who studied at Oxford and moves easily between the court and foreign capitals.

They favour a prime minister responsible to parliament, legal political associations, land reform for tenants and a market economy tied to the West. They fear that delay will bring revolution. Their leverage lies in ministries, embassies and the confidence of Western governments and donors.

3.name: Confederation of Ethiopian Labour Unions
3.text:
The Confederation of Ethiopian Labour Unions was legalized in 1963 and brings together unions of railway, textile, brewery, sugar and transport workers, with its centre in Addis Ababa and the Franco-Ethiopian railway towns.

CELU demands collective bargaining, minimum wages, job security and the right to strike, and keeps contacts with Western free trade unions. It avoids open challenges to the throne, but its strikes are growing in frequency. Its leverage lies in the railway, the factories of Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa and the ports of Assab and Massawa.

4.name: Mela Ityopia Sosialist Neqnaqe
4.text:
The All-Ethiopia Socialist Movement is a clandestine Marxist organization formed in 1968 by Ethiopian students and intellectuals in Europe, led by Haile Fida in Paris. It is small, secretive and has only scattered contacts inside the country.

MEISON calls for the overthrow of the feudal monarchy, land to the tiller, equality of nationalities and alignment with the socialist camp. It believes in a disciplined vanguard working through mass organizations. Its leverage lies in the student unions abroad and in a generation of graduates returning home.

5.name: University Students' Union of Addis Ababa
5.english: University Students' Union of Addis Ababa
5.text:
The University Students' Union of Addis Ababa leads the student movement at Haile Selassie I University. Its president Tilahun Gizaw was shot dead on 28 December 1969, and the protests that followed were crushed by troops on campus. In November 1969 Walleligne Makonnen raised the question of nationalities in the union's journal.

The students demand land to the tiller, an end to the monarchy, equality of nationalities and expulsion of American bases. Their leverage lies in strikes, demonstrations and influence over high-school youth.

6.name: Ye-Gojjam Shiftoch
6.text:
Ye-Gojjam Shiftoch are the peasant rebels of Gojjam who rose in 1968 against a new agricultural income tax and the land survey that came with it. The revolt forced the government to withdraw the tax and replace the provincial governor.

The rebels reject modern taxation, central officials and any interference in the ancestral rist land system. They are loyal to the Orthodox Church and suspicious of foreigners and Addis Ababa alike. Their leverage lies in arms, rugged terrain and a tradition of resistance the state has learned to fear.

7.name: Jebhat Tahrir Iritriya
7.text:
The Eritrean Liberation Front was founded in Cairo in 1960 and began armed struggle in 1961. Its chairman Idris Muhammad Adem leads the exile leadership, while the field army is being reorganized under a General Command after the Adobaha conference of 1969.

The ELF demands independence for Eritrea, whose federation was abolished in 1962. Its base lies among Muslim lowlanders, though Christian highland youth are joining. It is backed by Syria, Iraq and Sudan and opposes the American presence at Kagnew. Its leverage lies in guerrilla warfare and Arab support.

8.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Addis Ababa
8.english: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Addis Ababa
8.text:
The Dawoodi Bohra community of Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa consists of Gujarati merchant families who settled in Ethiopia since the late 19th century. It follows the Dai al-Mutlaq in Bombay and runs its own mosque and community institutions.

The community values commerce, education and loyalty to the ruler of the land, combined with strict religious observance. It keeps away from politics and relies on the Emperor's protection of foreign merchants. Its leverage lies in trade in the capital and the railway towns.

9.name: Ansar Ahl al-Bayt
9.text:
Ansar Ahl al-Bayt is a small devotional circle among Yemeni traders and dockworkers in Dire Dawa, Assab and Massawa, where Zaydi and Twelver Shia from Arabia have long lived in the shadow of Sunni and Christian majorities.

The circle looks to clerical authority, celebrates Ashura in private and keeps contacts with Najaf and the Zaydi highlands of Yemen. It dreams of a community guided by the descendants of the Prophet. It has no political weight, and its leverage lies only in Red Sea trade networks.

10.name: Ulama' Harar
10.text:
The Ulama of Harar are the scholars of the walled city that has been the centre of Islamic learning in the Horn of Africa for centuries. They administer mosques, shrines, Koranic schools and the sharia courts the empire allows Muslims for personal matters.

They seek recognition of Islam as an equal faith, Muslim holidays and access to state posts, while remaining loyal to the Emperor. They oppose radical and secessionist currents. Their leverage lies in the religious authority of Harar over Muslims of Hararghe, Wollo and Jimma.

11.name: Ahl at-Tawhid
11.text:
Ahl at-Tawhid are a few dozen young preachers returned from Saudi Arabia and the Hejaz to Harar, Jimma and Dessie, preaching a strict Islam in the shadow of an Orthodox Christian empire.

They denounce saint veneration, the Sufi orders and the scholars who serve the imperial order, and speak of a Muslim polity that would end Christian supremacy in the Horn. They have no organization, but they find a hearing among young Muslims excluded from state posts. Their leverage lies in Saudi money and Red Sea contacts.

12.name: Shabab al-Azhar
12.text:
Shabab al-Azhar are Ethiopian and Eritrean Muslims who studied at Al-Azhar in Cairo and returned with the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood and Islamic reform. They teach in Muslim schools of Addis Ababa, Harar and Asmara and write for small Arabic-language circles.

They call for Muslim education, Arabic teaching, equal rights for Muslims in state employment and a modern Islamic social ethic. They reject secession but sympathize with Eritrean grievances. Their leverage lies in schools, Egyptian scholarships and Muslim merchant patrons.

13.name: Ye-Minister Mekir Bet
13.text:
The Council of Ministers is the imperial cabinet, led since 1961 by Prime Minister Aklilu Habte-Wold, a French-trained lawyer and veteran diplomat. Ministers are appointed by and answerable to the Emperor, not to parliament.

The council runs a slow modernization: schools, roads, the Awash development and foreign loans, while avoiding land reform. It balances American military aid with non-aligned diplomacy and the Organization of African Unity seated in Addis Ababa. Its leverage lies in the ministries, budgets and daily access to the Emperor.

14.name: Ye-Ityopia Ortodoks Tewahedo Bete Kristiyan
14.text:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, autocephalous since 1959, is led by Patriarch Abuna Basilios. It is the established church of the empire, owns extensive lands and anoints the Solomonic emperors.

The church defends the Christian identity of the state, its lands and tithes, and the traditional order in the countryside. Its clergy are conservative and suspicious of students, Marxists and Protestant missions. Its leverage lies in tens of thousands of priests and monks, parish life in the highlands and its bond with the throne.

15.name: Mesafint
15.text:
Mesafint, the princes, are the great noble families who hold vast estates in Shewa, Gojjam, Begemder and the south, where tenants pay a large share of the harvest. Ras Asrate Kassa, governor of Eritrea and a pillar of the court, is among their foremost members.

They defend land tenure, tenancy rights for landlords and the privileges of rank, and block every tenant protection bill. They favour the American alliance and a strong throne. Their leverage lies in land, regional governorships and their kinship with the imperial family.

16.name: Addis Ababa Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Addis Ababa Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1947, unites importers, coffee exporters and merchants, among them many Armenian, Greek, Italian, Arab and Indian traders as well as a growing number of Ethiopians.

The chamber calls for lower tariffs, stable currency, credit for private business and an end to arbitrary licensing and monopolies granted to court favourites. It welcomes foreign investment. Its leverage lies in the coffee trade, the Mercato of Addis Ababa and the government's dependence on customs revenue.

17.name: Ethiopian Wildlife and Natural History Society
17.english: Ethiopian Wildlife and Natural History Society
17.text:
The Ethiopian Wildlife and Natural History Society was founded in 1966 by Ethiopian and foreign naturalists in Addis Ababa. It works alongside the young Wildlife Conservation Department, which is creating the first national parks in the Awash valley and the Simien mountains.

The society promotes protection of the walia ibex, Simien fox and mountain nyala, controls on hunting and the conservation of highland forests. Its members are teachers, foreign experts and educated townspeople. Its leverage lies in foreign support and imperial patronage of the parks.

18.name: Mecha and Tulama Self-Help Association
18.text:
The Mecha and Tulama Self-Help Association was founded in 1963 to build schools, roads and clinics for the Oromo of Shewa and beyond. Its rapid growth alarmed the court, and it was banned in 1967; its leader, General Tadesse Biru, is imprisoned.

The association called for equal citizenship for the Oromo, education in their own language, land for tenants and an end to discrimination in the army and civil service. Its leverage lies in the Oromo majority of the empire and in a network of former members in towns and the military.

19.name: Ethiopian Students Union in North America
19.english: Ethiopian Students Union in North America
19.text:
The Ethiopian Students Union in North America unites Ethiopian students at American and Canadian universities. Under the influence of the New Left and Chinese Marxism, it has moved from reformist nationalism to open calls for revolution, and its journal Challenge is read secretly at home.

ESUNA demands the overthrow of the monarchy, land to the tiller, self-determination of nationalities and an end to American bases, while distrusting Soviet orthodoxy. Its leverage lies in the future elite of the country now studying abroad.

20.name: Bale Insurgents
20.text:
The Bale insurgents have fought the imperial government in the southern lowlands since 1963. Led by Waqo Gutu, Oromo and Somali pastoralists and farmers rose against land grants to northern settlers, heavy taxes and the rule of Amhara officials.

The rebels demand the return of their lands, freedom from tribute and an end to Christian highland rule; many look to Somalia for arms and refuge. Years of counter-insurgency have worn them down. Their leverage lies in the remote terrain of Bale and support across the Somali border.

21.name: Yehager Fikir Mahber
21.text:
The Patriotic Association was founded in 1935 to rally the nation against the Italian invasion and is today a state-sponsored propaganda body with its own theatre in Addis Ababa. Around it gather veterans of the Patriot resistance and officials of the Ministry of Information.

The association celebrates the Emperor, the Orthodox faith, the unity of Greater Ethiopia and the victory at Adwa, and treats any regional or ethnic demand as treason. Its leverage lies in the press, radio, theatre and the official memory of the war against fascism.

22.name: Ye-Ityopia Nigusawi Tor Serawit
22.text:
The Imperial Ethiopian Armed Forces are the largest military in sub-Saharan Africa, equipped and trained largely by the United States, with Israeli advisers in counter-insurgency. They are fighting the ELF in Eritrea and the rebels of Bale, and garrison the Somali frontier.

The officer corps is loyal to the Emperor but divided between aristocratic generals and junior officers from the Harar military academy and Holeta, who resent low pay and corruption. Its leverage lies in its weapons and its role as the empire's last line of defence.

23.name: Sirwe Mengist Solomon
23.text:
The Solomonic dynasty, claiming descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, rules through Emperor Haile Selassie I, crowned in 1930 and restored after the Italian occupation in 1941. Crown Prince Asfa Wossen is heir. The 1955 constitution leaves sovereignty with the throne.

The Emperor governs as the elect of God, balances nobles, church, army and technocrats, and seeks prestige as father of African unity. He relies on American aid while courting both blocs. The dynasty's leverage lies in sacred legitimacy, control of appointments and Haile Selassie's personal authority.
